column2: Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa, and to Nara, the highest of men,
and to the goddess Sarasvatī as well, one should then recite the Jaya.
Ugraśravas, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa, a bard versed in the ancient lore, at the twelve-year sacrificial session of Śaunaka, the master of the house, in the Naimiṣa Forest,
came up to the brahmin seers of strict vows as they sat at their ease,
bowed low in humility, one day, the son of the bard.
When he had reached the hermitage, the dwellers of the Naimiṣa Forest,
the ascetics, gathered round him there to hear his wondrous tales.
Greeting all those hermits with joined palms,
he asked after the growth of their austerities, and the good ones welcomed him.
Then, when all those ascetics had sat down,
Lomaharṣaṇa's son humbly took the seat that was shown him.
Seeing him seated at his ease and rested,
a certain seer there asked him, to set the tales going:

these are the Pāṇḍavas." So saying, the hermits vanished.
Seeing the Pāṇḍavas presented by them, the Kauravas
and the cultured classes and the townsmen cried out loudly for joy.
Some said, "They are not his"; others, "They are his";
others, "Since Pāṇḍu is long dead, how are they his?"

Welcome in every way! By good fortune we see Pāṇḍu's offspring.
75.2	Let welcome be spoken! — such words were heard on every side.
When that clamour died away, making all the directions resound,
a tumultuous noise arose from beings who could not be seen.
A rain of flowers, sweet scents, the sound of conches and drums
were there at the Pārthas' entry; it was like a marvel.
And from the delight of all the townsmen at this, born of joy,
a great sound rose there, touching heaven, increasing their fame.
They too, having studied all the Vedas and treatises of many kinds,
the Pāṇḍavas, lived there, honoured, fearing nothing from anywhere.
The subjects were pleased by Yudhiṣṭhira's purity,
by Bhīmasena's steadfastness and Arjuna's valour,
by Kuntī's service to her elders and the modesty of the twins;
the whole world was content with their heroism and their virtue.
Then, in a gathering of kings, the maiden who chose her husband herself,
Kṛṣṇā, Arjuna won, having done a deed most hard to do.
From then on he was honoured in this world by all who bear the bow,
and in battles he became hard to look at, like the sun.
He, having conquered all the kings and all the great hosts,
Arjuna brought the king the Rājasūya, the great rite.
Rich in food, rich in fees, endowed with every virtue,
the great rite Rājasūya was achieved by Yudhiṣṭhira,
through the good counsel of Vāsudeva and the strength of Bhīma and Arjuna,
having had Jarāsaṃdha killed, and the Caidya, proud of his strength.
To Duryodhana came the gifts of homage from every side:
gems, gold, jewels, cattle, elephants, horses and riches.
Seeing that prosperity of the Pāṇḍavas so abundant,
a very great anger, born of envy, arose in him.
And the hall like a flying palace, well built by Maya,
presented to the Pāṇḍavas — seeing it, he burned with grief,
the hall where he was laughed at, as if stumbling in confusion,
in front of Vāsudeva, by Bhīma, as though he were low-born.
Though he enjoyed pleasures of many kinds and jewels of many kinds,
he was reported to Dhṛtarāṣṭra as pale, sallow and thin.
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, fond of his son, allowed the dicing;
hearing of it, a great anger arose in Vāsudeva.
He was not much pleased in his mind, yet he approved the quarrels,
and he overlooked the terrible wrongs, the dicing and the rest, as they grew.
Setting aside Vidura, Droṇa, Bhīṣma and Kṛpa, son of Śaradvat,
in that tumultuous war the warriors slew one another.
When the sons of Pāṇḍu were winning, hearing news most unwelcome,
knowing the mind of Duryodhana, of Karṇa and of Śakuni,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, after pondering long, spoke these words to Saṃjaya:

Hear everything from me, Saṃjaya; you should not find fault with me.
